summary: Defines the syntax and semantics of relative Uniform Resource Locators, which let a reference inherit context from a known base URL instead of repeating everything. It was a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 3986.

eli5.summary: Instead of giving your full home address, you can say next door, and everyone knows which street you mean.

questions: how do relative urls resolve against a base
how do dot dot segments work in urls
subtitle: How a short link like ../g gets turned into a full URL by borrowing context from a base URL.

tldr.problem: Documents full of absolute URLs repeat the scheme, host and path prefix everywhere, and break whenever the document tree moves or is served over a different scheme.
tldr.mechanism: A relative URL leaves out a prefix and inherits it from a base URL. The RFC defines the generic syntax, how a base URL is established, and a step-by-step algorithm that resolves a relative URL to absolute form.
tldr.outcome: This is the origin of the relative-link rules used with URLs. RFC 1808 has since been obsoleted by RFC 3986, and was also updated by RFC 2368 and RFC 2396.

today: RFC 1808 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3986. It was also updated by RFC 2368 and RFC 2396, and it itself updated RFC 1738.

sections.title: Why Relative URLs Exist
sections.content:
An absolute URL carries the scheme, the network location and the path. Inside a document, much of that is already known from how the document was fetched. Relative URLs let an embedded reference inherit that context instead of repeating it in every link.

Documents in one tree mostly point at other documents in the same tree or at the same site. Relative links make the tree partly independent of where it lives: the RFC notes that one set of hypertext documents can be reachable through the file, http and ftp schemes at once, and a whole tree can be moved without changing the embedded URLs. It is a companion to RFC 1738, which defines absolute URLs.
sections.eli5: If all your friends live on your street, you can just say 'number 5' instead of the whole address. And if the street gets a new name, nobody has to rewrite their notes.

sections.title: Generic Syntax and Parsing
sections.content:
To resolve relative references, the RFC describes a single generic-RL syntax with six components: scheme://net_loc/path;params?query#fragment. Every component except the scheme may be absent. The fragment is not considered part of the URL, but a parser must still recognise it and set it aside.

Parsing works in a fixed order: first the fragment (introduced by the hash sign), then the scheme (before the first colon), then the network location (after a leading //), then the query (after the first ?), then the parameters (after the first ;). What remains is the path, and the parser must remember whether it began with a slash so it can tell relative paths from absolute ones.

Some schemes never work with relative URLs: mailto, news and telnet. Others, including file, ftp, http and nntp, can always be parsed with the generic syntax. New schemes meant for relative use are recommended to follow it too.
sections.eli5: A web address is like a sentence with parts in a set order. The computer reads the parts one at a time from the end to the front and puts each in its own box.

sections.title: Establishing the Base URL
sections.content:
A relative URL means nothing without a base URL. The RFC lists four ways to find it, in order of precedence, with the innermost winning:

  1. A base URL embedded in the document content, or in a message header such as Base: <URL:http://www.ics.uci.edu/Test/a/b/c>.
  2. The base URL of the entity that encloses the document, such as a MIME multipart message.
  3. The URL used to retrieve the document. After a redirect, this is the last URL used.
  4. Otherwise the base is the empty string, and every embedded URL is treated as absolute.

The RFC stresses that the distributor of a document is responsible for making sure its base URL can be established. Relative URLs cannot be used reliably when it is not well defined.
sections.eli5: 'Next door' only makes sense if you know where the speaker is standing. The base URL is the place you are standing, and there is a set order for figuring that out.

sections.title: The Resolution Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example algorithm in seven steps. In short: if the base is empty, or the embedded URL starts with a scheme, it is already absolute. An entirely empty reference means the base URL itself. Otherwise the embedded URL inherits the base scheme, then the network location unless it has its own, and then the path.

A path that starts with a slash is not relative. An empty path inherits the base path, and also the parameters and query if none were given. A relative path replaces the last segment of the base path, and then . and .. segments are removed in a defined order.

The algorithm is offered so implementations can be tested against its output. Implementing the algorithm itself is not required, so a system may merge path segments with stacks instead of string matching.

Parameters do not affect how relative paths resolve, and the fragment is inherited from the base only when the whole embedded URL is empty.
sections.eli5: It is a recipe: start from the base address, throw away the last bit, stick on what the link says, and cancel out any 'go up one folder' steps.

sections.title: Examples and Recommended Practice
sections.content:
The RFC resolves many references against the base http://a/b/c/d;p?q#f. Normal cases include g becoming http://a/b/c/g, ../g becoming http://a/b/g and /g becoming http://a/g.

Abnormal cases are unlikely but parsers should still handle them consistently. Extra .. segments cannot change the network location, and . or .. are special only when they are complete path segments, so g. and ..g are ordinary names.

On practice, a path containing a colon, such as this:that, would be mistaken for a scheme if it starts a relative reference. Write ./this:that (preferred) or escape the colon as this%3Athat. The RFC also advises against the ;type=d parameter on ftp URLs in contexts that allow relative URLs. Its security section says there are no security considerations in using or parsing relative URLs, though the resolved absolute URL carries those of RFC 1738.
sections.eli5: A few tricks have surprising answers, like a folder named 'g.' being just a normal name. And if a name has a colon in it, put './' in front so nobody mistakes it for something else.
